subject: Computer Networking
title: The Telegraph: First Network
description: A quick win: understand The Telegraph: First Network.

hook.text: In 1844, Morse tapped a message from Washington to Baltimore. Instant long-distance communication was born.

buildup.text: The telegraph used electrical signals over copper wire. Operators encoded letters as dots and dashes.

discovery.text: By 1866, a transatlantic cable connected Europe and America. A message that once took weeks arrived in minutes.

twist.text: The telegraph network had routing, relay stations, and standard codes — the same concepts modern networks use.

climax.text: It transformed business, journalism, and war. Decisions that took weeks could now be made in hours.

punchline.text: The telegraph was the internet of the 1800s.

quiz.question: What year was the first successful telegraph message sent?

details.summary: The telegraph, invented in the 1830s and 1840s, was the first long-distance electronic communication network. It transmitted coded messages through electrical signals over wires, connecting cities and continents.
details.whyItMatters: The telegraph invented the very idea of sending information electronically over distance. Every network since, including the internet, builds on principles the telegraph established.
takeaways: The telegraph was the world's first electronic communication network
Morse code was the first standardized communication protocol
Telegraph networks pioneered routing, switching, and addressing

faq.question: How was the telegraph a precursor to the internet?
faq.answer: It introduced electronic signal transmission, standardized protocols, dedicated network infrastructure, message routing through relay stations, and the concept of a global connected network. Undersea telegraph cables were the ancestors of modern fiber optic cables.

faq.question: When did the telegraph network peak?
faq.answer: The telegraph network peaked in the late 1800s after transatlantic cables were laid in 1866. By the 1870s, most major cities worldwide were connected. The telephone gradually replaced it for personal communication, but telegrams remained common into the 1960s.
